quotes.text: It isn't an Azure product you turn on. It isn't a compliance badge you earn. It's a decision framework for designing and running a workload that can hold up over time.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clears up the most common misconception about what the Well-Architected Framework is.

quotes.text: So the question isn't how much reliability can we buy. It is what level of reliability does this workload need and what are we willing to support?
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reframes reliability as a business decision instead of a shopping list.

quotes.text: A cheap design that cannot recover when needed is expensive when it fails, so phrase the goal carefully. Don't say, make this workload cheaper. Say remove waste while keeping the agreed service recovery and security levels.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Gives a concrete, reusable way to phrase cost goals without sacrificing protection.

quotes.text: Performance isn't about buying the biggest machine. It is about measuring the work, finding the slow part and meeting the promise when it counts.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Summarises the performance efficiency pillar in one memorable principle.

quotes.text: The team can improve a written promise. It can't improve assumptions that live in separate people's heads.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Makes the case for writing down workload requirements before reviewing them.

takeaways: The Azure Well-Architected Framework is a decision framework for one workload at a time, while the Cloud Adoption Framework prepares the shared company-wide foundation.
Each of the five pillars forces trade-offs, so goals like cost reduction should always be phrased together with the agreed recovery and security targets.
Start small with one important workload, run the Azure Well-Architected review and turn its recommendations into an owned, prioritized backlog.
hook: Unexpected Azure bills, over-permissive apps and late-night outages often come from the decisions around a service, not the service itself. This episode explains the Azure Well-Architected Framework and its five pillars for cloud architects, developers and IT teams. You learn how to weigh trade-offs and run a practical review on one workload.
